# The Final Step

> "Stand firm therefore in the liberty by which Christ has made us free, and don't be entangled again with a yoke of bondage."
>
> — Galatians 5:1

You've settled the timing. You're ready for the final step.

It is not a final session. Chapter 1 promised you there would be no "one last time", and there isn't. Nobody sins once more for old times' sake on his way out of a sin. And you don't need to. If you've carried on as normal while you read, your last time is already behind you. You didn't mark it with a ceremony, and that's the right send-off for a thing that was never worth anything.

(This is the one place where this book leaves EasyPeasy's path on purpose. EasyPeasy, following Allen Carr, ends with a last deliberate session, entered with eyes open. Many people have found that useful for porn and for cigarettes. We don't do it. Nobody takes leave of a sin by committing it carefully.)

The final step is a prayer. Before you pray it, check the two essentials.

1. **Are you certain?**
2. **Are you excited?** Do you have a sense of doom and gloom, or the feeling of a man about to do something marvellous?

If you have doubts on either count, stop here and re-read the book first. There's no hurry and no shame in it.

Nobody *decides* to fall into this trap. You wandered in as a boy. But the trap is built to hold you for life, and nobody wanders out of it. Getting out takes one clear, positive decision, and you're about to make it.

## "But I've made this vow before" {-}

Of course you have, and you broke it every time. You may be afraid of breaking another.

Look at what you were vowing then. You promised to go without something you still wanted. That was a vow against yourself, and half of you never signed it. Today is different, because there's nothing left that you want from it. You're only putting into words what has already happened in your head.

There's nothing to fear either. At the very worst you fail, and then you're no worse off than you are today. You have nothing to lose and a great deal to gain.

But don't think about failing at all. This time you aren't climbing by willpower. You're walking out through an open door, and you can enjoy the walk. If you're a Christian, you also have something stronger than your own word to stand on. Heath Lambert wrote it of pornography, and it holds for every form lust takes: "Jesus' grace to change you is stronger than pornography's power to destroy you."

And if what holds you back is the feeling that you've failed too often to come back again, hear a man who felt exactly that. He pictures the prodigal son halfway home, protesting that he still smells of the pigsty, and the Father answering with two words. "But God, I still smell like yesterday. Just come." He adds, for every man reading: "You're not too dirty. You're not too far."

A word about vows. Jesus had no time for elaborate oaths. "But let your 'Yes' be 'Yes' and your 'No' be 'No.'" That's the kind of vow this is: a plain No that you mean.

## The prayer {-}

Here are the instructions.

**1. Go somewhere you can be alone and speak out loud.** Kneel if you're able. A man's body teaches his mind what's going on.

**2. Pray this.** Use your own words if you prefer, but don't make it long or clever.

> Father, I confess it.
>
> I have used my body, my eyes and my mind for lust. I have looked at women as things to use. I have done it in secret, told myself it was nothing, and hidden it from the people who love me. It was sin, and I am sorry.
>
> Forgive me, as you promised you would. Make me clean.
>
> Today I am finished with it. I will not masturbate again. I will not watch porn again. I will not use a woman, or let lust decide what I do about one. I will not feed lust with my eyes or my imagination. Whether I find it easy or hard, my answer is No.
>
> I can't keep this by my own strength, and I'm not going to try. Keep me. Make me a man who can be trusted, and make me fit for whatever you made me for. Then show me the man I am to go back for.
>
> Thank you that I am forgiven. Thank you that I am free.
>
> In Jesus's name. Amen.

**3. If you're not a believer, say it out loud anyway.** I mean that. Address it to God in case he's listening, or to the empty room, or to the man you intend to be. Leave off the first and last lines if you honestly can't say them. But say the confession and say the vow, aloud and on your feet or on your knees. A decision you've only thought is easy to un-think. One you've spoken has been heard, if only by you.

**4. Then stand up and say it:**

**"YES! I'M FREE!"**

Shout it if the neighbours can stand it.

Don't get up thinking "I must never do that again" or "I'm not allowed any more". Those are a prisoner's sentences. Get up thinking, "Isn't it wonderful? I never have to do that again. I'm free."

Do it now.

## The next few days {-}

For a little while the Little Monster will still be about. You may notice him only as a vague feeling that you'd like to do *something*. Chapter 21 called this the leftover itch. Because he takes a few weeks to starve, men assume they'll crave for a few weeks and will need willpower to hold out. They won't. Your body isn't asking for anything. The itch is only a feeling until your mind decides what to call it.

So when the feeling comes, your mind has a choice. It can take the feeling for what it is: an empty, restless twinge. The habit itself put it there, and every past session kept it alive. So it can answer: "YES! I'M FREE!"

Or it can call the feeling a craving and start pining.

Think how stupid the second choice would be. A man says, "I never want to do that again," and then spends his life saying, "I'd love to, just once." That's the willpower quitter. He is always longing for the very thing he prays he'll never do. No wonder he's miserable.

## Let it ring {-}

A surgeon turned writer named Maxwell Maltz had a picture for this, and it's worth carrying with you.

Imagine you're sitting in an armchair and the telephone rings. All your life you've jumped up to answer it. Today you stay in the chair. You can hear it perfectly well. You're not pretending it isn't ringing, and you're not gripping the armrests. You just don't get up.

Two things follow. First, the ringing has no power of its own. A bell is a noise in the air and can't lift a man out of a chair. It only ever moved you because you'd formed the habit of obeying it. Second, not answering takes no effort. You aren't wrestling the phone. You're doing nothing at all, and doing it comfortably.

Every cue you'll meet is that telephone. It may be the empty house, the photo in the feed, the bed at midnight, the bad day or the message from her. Let it ring. It will stop.

## You are already free {-}

Only two things can make this hard: doubting and waiting. So never doubt the decision. You know it's right. If you start to question it, you put yourself where you can't win. You'll be miserable if you don't, and worse if you do.

Ask what you're actually trying to achieve. It isn't simply "never to do any of it again". Plenty of ex-users manage that and feel robbed until they die. Think instead about the man who has never had the habit. He isn't different from you because he resists. He doesn't want it. He has no craving, and he isn't using any willpower.

That's what you're after, and it's entirely in your power. You don't have to wait for it either. You didn't become that man gradually. You became him when you said Amen.

**YOU ARE ALREADY A FREE MAN.**

And you'll stay a happy one, on these conditions:

1. Never doubt your decision.
2. Don't wait to "become" free. You are free. If you wait, you're only waiting for nothing to happen.
3. Don't try not to think about it, and don't sit watching for the moment of revelation. Either one will turn it into a phobia.
4. Use no substitutes.
5. See men who are still in the trap for what they are, and pity them. Never envy them.

On good days and bad, don't change your life because you've stopped. If you do, you'll turn a non-sacrifice into a real one. You haven't given up living, and you haven't given up anything. You've been healed of something and let out of somewhere. The weeks will go by, and your energy and your conscience will recover. Your good days will be better and your bad days milder than they ever were.

And whenever the thought of it crosses your mind, tomorrow or in forty years, think:

**"YES! I'M FREE!"**

## A final warning {-}

No man in this trap, offered the chance to go back to the day before he started, knowing what he knows now, would start. Yet men who have walked out and lived happily for years go back in. I hope this book has made stopping easy for you. But a man who finds stopping easy can find starting again just as easy.

DON'T FALL FOR THAT.

However long you've been free, and however sure you are that you could never be caught again, keep one lifelong rule: not once, for any reason. A lonely anniversary doesn't count as a reason. Nor does "to help me sleep", or "just to see". Bonhoeffer knew why the rule has to be permanent: "In our members there is a slumbering inclination toward desire, which is both sudden and fierce." The inclination is asleep, so don't wake it.

The rule is strict, and the grace is real. If you ever do fall, a short chapter called If You Slip tells you what to do. Don't plan on needing it.

Remember what that one time would do for you. It would do nothing. You'd have no itch for it to relieve, and you'd feel foolish and flat. But it would wake the Little Monster, and a small voice in your head would say, "Another." Then you'd have two choices: be miserable for a while as he starves again, or start the whole dreary chain from the beginning.

Paul wrote his sentence to people who were already free. He didn't tell them to try to get free. He told them to stand firm in it, and not to be "entangled again".

You're free, so stand firm.
